title: Zeolite-based bifunctional catalysts for the single step synthesis of dimethyl ether from CO-rich synthesis gas
abstract: Zeolite-based bifunctional catalysts for the production of dimethyl ether (DME) from CO-rich synthesis gas (H2:CO = 1) were prepared via various preparation methods including co-precipitation–impregnation, impregnation, co-precipitation sedimentation and oxalate co-precipitation. The catalysts comprise a Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 component for methanol formation and zeolite H-MFI 400 as acidic component for methanol dehydration to DME. An admixed catalyst system was used as reference and all catalysts were characterized by SEM-EDX, XRF, N2-physisorption, XRD, H2-TPR, NH3-TPD, N2O-pulse chemisorption and TEM. The catalysts were tested in a continuously operating laboratory plant and the experiments revealed that the synthesis strategy strongly influences catalyst properties and hence catalyst activity. Especially a bifunctional catalyst prepared via oxalate co-precipitation proved to be highly active and could compete with conventional admixed catalyst systems. High CO-conversion and a high DME-selectivity could be reached. Catalyst characterization revealed that high Cu surface areas, small Cu particle sizes and a high number of moderate acidic sites are crucial to achieve maximum catalytic performance.
paragraphs: Globally, the demand for fossil feedstocks is dramatically increasing coming along with a shortage of resources and an enormous environmental impact. Thus, the use of renewable resources is of steadily growing interest. Renewables can substitute fossil raw materials in numerous applications such as materials development, energy supply and chemicals as well as fuels production. Regarding fuels production from biomass, numerous strategies are known (Fig. 1) and some biofuels are already employed even on large scale [1]. Prominent examples are fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) [2], e.g. biodiesel obtained by transesterification of rapeseed oil with methanol (rapeseed methyl ester, RME), pure or hydrotreated vegetable oils (PVOs and HVOs) [3], ethanol produced by fermentation of sugars and starch [4] or biomethane generated by anaerobic digestion of biomass [5].

Production of synthesis gas from biomass is another option, which makes a series of fuels accessible (Fig. 1), e.g. hydrogen via the water-gas shift (WGS) reaction [6], synthetic natural gas (SNG) via methanation reactions [7], or hydrocarbons by Fischer–Tropsch reactions [8]. Another strategy is the production of methanol employing Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 (CZA) catalysts [9]. Methanol can serve as raw material for a variety of chemicals [10] and fuels such as gasoline and diesel [11], [12]. Further possibilities for methanol processing are its homologation to higher alcohols, production of hydrogen via reforming and its reaction with isobutylene to MTBE [13].

Methanol can also be converted to dimethyl ether (DME), which is a promising alternative fuel [14]. Regarding physical properties, DME is very similar to liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) [15] and it is used in domestic applications. It exhibits a very high cetane number of about 55 and can also be used as diesel substitute without extensive modification of the diesel engine. Another advantage of DME is its comparatively clean combustion thus reducing soot formation and emission [16]. The production and use of DME as transportation fuel have been investigated within the European BioDME project, which has been moved forward by a consortium of Chemrec, ETC, Haldor Topsøe, Total, Preem, Volvo, Delphi, and the Swedish Energy Agency [17]. The process is based on gasification of black liquor from the pulp industry and the resulting synthesis gas is first converted to methanol. Subsequently, methanol is dehydrated to DME employing solid acid catalysts. Very recently, commercialization of DME-powered trucks in North America was announced [18].

Apart from DME synthesis via methanol dehydration, direct production from synthesis gas (Synthesis gas-To-DME, STD) is an attractive option [19], [20]. This strategy is favorable in the case of biomass-derived synthesis gases, which are CO-rich with typical H2:CO-ratios around 1 and also lower. According to thermodynamics, the STD-process allows for higher CO-conversions compared to conventional methanol synthesis followed by dehydration to DME. Catalyst systems, which catalyze simultaneously methanol formation, methanol dehydration and the WGS reaction, are employed in STD-synthesis. Thus, intermediary formed water from methanol dehydration is immediately consumed via the WGS reaction. The single reactions and the overall reaction can be described by the following equations:2 CO + 4 H2 → 2 CH3OH2 CH3OH → CH3OCH3 + H2OCO + H2O → H2 + CO2Overall:3 CO + 3 H2 → CH3OCH3 + CO2

So far, industrial production of DME is carried out by methanol dehydration. However, the STD-process has been implemented on pilot-scale. For instance, JFE Holdings tested the synthesis of DME from natural gas-based synthesis gas in a 5 t/d pilot plant in 1999 [21]. Furthermore, a 10 t/d pilot plant for the STD-process has been constructed by the Korea Gas Corporation in 2004 [22].

Bifunctional catalyst systems that combine active sites for methanol generation and methanol dehydration in one compound can be used as catalysts for the STD-process instead of the classical admixed system, in which a methanol catalyst and a solid acid are physically mixed. The preparation and the properties of bifunctional catalysts have been described by many authors [23], [24], [25], [26], [27], [28], [29]. However, there are different opinions on the efficiency of bifunctional catalysts in comparison to admixed systems. Sun et al. prepared bifunctional catalysts by co-precipitation sedimentation of a ZrO2-doped CZA-component on an H-ZSM 5 zeolite [23], [24]. According to them, bifunctional catalysts lead to high CO-conversions because the two types of active sites are in close contact with each other. This enables the generation of DME directly from an adsorbed methoxy-species without the intermediary synthesis of methanol. Ge et al. also concluded that both active sites need to be in close contact so that a synergistic effect can be achieved, which leads to higher catalytic activity [30]. However, Ge et al. stressed that coverage of both active sites during catalyst synthesis needs to be avoided. A coverage of the active sites leads to a drop in activity due to the synthesis of inactive species and due to a decrease in active surface area. García-Trenco et al. stated that admixed catalyst systems are superior to bifunctional systems [31]. According to them, the preparation procedure of bifunctional catalysts can lead to a decrease of surface area due to a blockage of pores. However, they also stated that further interactions between the two active components, which have not been elucidated yet, influence catalyst activity as well. These examples show that a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms and interactions between the two active components in admixed as well as bifunctional catalysts is necessary. Furthermore, the influence of catalyst composition and features on catalytic activity should be studied more in detail so that a comparison of catalysts independent of the respective preparation method will be possible.

In previous work [32] several catalyst systems for the direct synthesis of DME from CO-rich synthesis gas were investigated and systems composed of CZA catalysts for methanol synthesis and WGS reaction as well as zeolite H-MFI 400 for methanol dehydration revealed high efficiency. Within the work described here bifunctional catalyst systems based on H-MFI 400 were prepared and characterized more in detail and the influence of synthesis strategy on catalyst features and activity was investigated. The preparation methods are similar to those reported by Ge et al. [30] and Moradi et al. [33]. As distinguished from these activities, additional preparation methods were employed and the zeolite H-MFI 400 was used as support. For the catalyst testing, a simulated biomass-derived synthesis gas was applied (H2:CO = 1:1). Moreover, this work focuses on the correlation between catalyst properties and catalyst activity.
Five systems were prepared and investigated of whom four were bifunctional catalysts (CZA-Z-CF, CZA-Z-IP, CZA-Z-CS, CZA-Z-OX) and the fifth was an admixed system that was used as a reference (CZA-Z).

CZA-Z consisted of a mechanically mixed system with the zeolite H-MFI 400 Extrudate (Si/Al = 200; Süd-Chemie AG) and a self-prepared CuO/ZnO/Al2O3-catalyst (CZA) in a weight ratio of 1:1. CZA was prepared by dissolving 5.85 g Cu(NO3)2 · 3H2O (21.20 mmol), 4.48 g Zn(NO3)2 · 6H2O (15.05 mmol) and 1.29 g Al(NO3)3 · 9H2O (3.43 mmol) in 50 ml deionized water. This solution was slowly co-precipitated at 70 °C with a 1 M Na2CO3-solution into 100 ml of deionized water. The pH was kept at 7 and the mixture was aged for 1 h. The light-blue precipitate was washed thoroughly with deionized water and dried at 80 °C for 12 h. Finally, the light-blue powder was calcined under air for 4 h at 350 °C with a heating rate of 175 °C/h. A black solid was obtained.

Catalyst CZA-Z-CF was prepared by dissolving 5.85 g Cu(NO3)2 · 3H2O (21.20 mmol), 4.48 g Zn(NO3)2 · 6H2O (15.05 mmol) and 1.29 g Al(NO3)3 · 9H2O (3.43 mmol) in 50 ml deionized water. This solution was slowly co-precipitated at 70 °C with a 1 M Na2CO3-solution into a suspension of 2.50 g grounded H-MFI 400 in 100 ml deionized water. The pH was kept at 7 and the mixture was aged for 1 h. The light-blue precipitate was washed thoroughly with deionized water and dried at 80 °C for 12 h. Finally, the light-blue powder was calcined under air for 4 h at 350 °C with a heating rate of 175 °C/h. A dark-gray solid was obtained.

A solution of 5.85 g Cu(NO3)2 · 3H2O (21.20 mmol), 4.48 g Zn(NO3)2 · 6H2O (15.05 mmol) and 1.29 g Al(NO3)3 · 9H2O (3.43 mmol) in 10 ml deionized water was given to a suspension of 2.50 g grounded H-MFI 400 in 15 ml deionized water. The mixture was stirred for 1 h at 70 °C and subsequently water was evaporated at 120 °C. The residue was dried at 80 °C for 12 h. Finally, the light-blue powder was calcined under air for 4 h at 350 °C with a heating rate of 175 °C/h. A gray solid was obtained.

Cu(NO3)2 · 3H2O (21.20 mmol), 4.48 g Zn(NO3)2 · 6H2O (15.05 mmol) and 1.29 g Al(NO3)3 · 9H2O (3.43 mmol) were dissolved in 50 ml deionized water and co-precipitated at 70 °C with a 1 M Na2CO3-solution into 100 ml of deionized water. The pH was kept at 7 and the mixture was aged for 1 h. The light-blue precipitate was washed thoroughly with deionized water. Subsequently, a suspension of the precipitate in 50 ml deionized water was prepared and given to a suspension of 2.50 g grounded H-MFI 400 in 100 ml deionized water. The mixture was stirred for 1 h at 70 °C following washing with deionized water. Afterwards, the residue was dried at 80 °C for 12 h and then calcined under air for 4 h at 350 °C with a heating rate of 175 °C/h. A dark-gray solid was obtained.

A 1 M solution of the metal nitrates (5.85 g Cu(NO3)2 · 3H2O (21.20 mmol), 4.48 g Zn(NO3)2 · 6H2O (15.05 mmol), 1.29 g Al(NO3)3 · 9H2O (3.43 mmol) in 42.68 ml deionized water) was mixed to a stirred suspension of 2.50 g grounded H-MFI 400 in 100 ml deionized water. The mixture was then cooled down to 0 °C and a solution of 8.655 g oxalic acid (96.13 mmol) in 121.58 ml ethanol was added dropwise. Afterwards, the mixture was aged for 1 h at 70 °C followed by evaporation of water at 120 °C. The residue was dried at 80 °C for 12 h and then calcined under air for 4 h at 350 °C with a heating rate of 175 °C/h. A black solid was obtained.

Metal loadings were determined by SEM-EDX and XRF. The EDX analysis was carried out employing an INCAPentaFET-x3 unit from Oxford Instruments on several locations of the catalysts and SEM images were recorded with a FESEM DSM 982 Gemini microscope (ZEISS) equipped with a backscatter detector. XRF analyses were carried out employing a SIEMENS SRS 303 sequence-spectrometer and the obtained data were evaluated with the Siemens SemiQuant 3000 software 2.0. Rh was used as radiation-source with an accelerating voltage of 20–60 kV (at 5 mA) and a flow meter as well as a scintillation counter were used as detectors.

The specific surface area (BET; p/p0 = x − y), total pore volume (p/p0 = x) and micropore surface (V–t-method, p/p0 = x − y) were determined by N2-physisorption using a Quantachrome Nova 2000e instrument.

XRD diffractograms were recorded using a PANalytical X'PERT-PRO diffractometer. Cu-Kα-X-radiation (0.154 nm) was employed and diffractograms were taken in a 1 h measurement over a 2θ range from 5° to 120°. The average crystallite size of the reduced Cu species was determined by the Scherrer equation with a correction for the instrumental broadening.

H2-TPR, NH3-TPD and N2O-pulse chemisorption were carried out using an AutoChem 2950 HP device from Micromeritics. H2-TPR was used to investigate reducibility of the catalysts. The samples were dried at 200 °C while under Ar, cooled down and then exposed to a diluted H2 atmosphere and heated up to 300 °C with 2 °C/min. The H2 uptake was recorded employing a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). NH3-TPD was employed to determine the acidity of the respective systems. The samples were dried at 300 °C while under He and after cooling down saturated with NH3 for 90 min. Afterwards, the samples were heated up to 800 °C in a He-flow. The release of NH3 was recorded by a TCD-detector. For determination of the specific Cu surface area N2O-pulse chemisorption was applied. The samples were reduced by H2-TPR as described above. At 60 °C pulses of N2O were given into the sample cell. Redundant N2O was collected in a cold trap and the evolved N2 was detected and recorded by the TCD-detector. The Cu surface area was calculated by assuming a surface density of 1.46 · 1019 Cu atoms/m2 [34].

Electron microscopy (transmission electron microscopy, TEM; scanning electron microscopy with high angle annular detector, STEM-HAADF; high resolution transmission electron microscopy, HRTEM) experiments and elemental analysis (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, EDX) were carried out employing a FEI Tecnai F20 ST TEM (operating voltage 200 kV) equipped with a field emission gun and EDAX EDS X-ray spectrometer [Si(Li) detecting unit, super ultra thin window, active area 30 mm2, resolution 135 eV (at 5.9 keV)]. For TEM analysis, the calcined catalysts were initially suspended in isopropanol. A small droplet of the catalyst suspension was deposited onto holey carbon-filmed copper grids (for HRTEM imaging) and carbon-filmed nickel grids (for EDX analysis) and finally air dried.

The catalyst screening was carried out in a continuously operating laboratory plant (Fig. 2). Core of the laboratory plant was a fixed-bed reactor with a volume of 60.3 ml, which was designed for pressures up to 100 bar and temperatures up to 450 °C. Gases were dosed by Mass Flow Controllers (MFC) and all gas flows were analyzed by an online-GC (HP 6890, Agilent) with two columns (RT®-U-BOND and RT-Msieve 5A, RESTEK) and two detectors (TCD and FID). For all reactions 2 g of each catalyst system with a particle size between 80 and 355 μm was placed in the reactor. Reduction of CuO to the active species Cu0 took place in a reducing atmosphere (2% H2 in Ar) while heating up to 240 °C with 17 °C/h. Afterwards, the gas flow was switched to pure H2 and the temperature was increased to 250 °C within 1 h. After keeping the system for 2 h under these conditions it was rinsed with Ar and subjected to pressure (p = 51 bar). A gas mixture containing (H2 + CO):(Ar + N2) with a ratio of 3:7 was employed and a WHSV of 4.19 h− 1 was adjusted. The H2:CO-ratio was 1:1 and the Ar:N2-ratio was 6:1. At first, metal loadings of each catalyst and specific BET surface areas were determined (Table 1). Although one and the same amount of reactants was applied for each system, composition slightly differs. Catalyst CZA-Z-CS for example contains a higher amount of CuO compared to the other systems. In general, catalyst composition in terms of the CuO:ZnO:Al2O3:SiO2 ratio is roughly 30:20:20:30 wt.%. This ratio, i.e. a high percentage of the acid component, was chosen to ensure a sufficient amount of acidic sites and thus maximum conversion of methanol to DME.

The surface areas of the bifunctional catalysts also differ from each other. While the reference system CZA-Z exhibits a surface area of 195 m2/g, CZA-Z-OX shows the highest area reaching 205 m2/g. Concerning the other catalysts, only the surface area of CZA-Z-CF is in the same range and a remarkable decrease is observed regarding CZA-Z-CS and CZA-Z-IP.

To investigate reducibility, H2-TPR measurements were carried out (Fig. 3). Compared to the reference catalyst CZA, which exhibits a uniform reduction peak at a temperature of 197 °C, the reduction behavior of the bifunctional catalysts differs. The main reduction peaks of catalysts CZA-Z-CF (Tm = 163 °C) and CZA-Z-CS (Tm = 149 °C) are shifted to much lower temperatures and thus, both catalysts are reduced more readily than CZA-Z-IP (Tm = 192 °C) and CZA-Z-OX (Tm = 193 °C) [30], [35]. The presence of shoulders and additional peaks indicates different Cu species and therefore inhomogeneous distribution of CuO. Catalysts CZA-Z-CF and CZA-Z-CS show more than one reduction peak, whereas CZA-Z-OX shows a comparatively uniform reduction curve. The common opinion is that shoulders at lower temperatures can be ascribed to the reduction of well-dispersed CuO and the main peak is attributed to the reduction of bulk CuO [35], [36], [37]. This could be the case for CZA-Z-IP that shows a shoulder at temperatures below its main peak at 192 °C. Catalysts CZA-Z-CF, CZA-Z-IP and CZA-Z-CS show peaks and shoulders, that appear at higher temperatures compared to their respective Tm value. In these cases, there might be a consecutive reduction of Cu2 + first to Cu+ and finally to Cu0 [38]. Such high temperature reduction peaks may also be ascribed to the reduction of copper-aluminates [39].

Results of NH3-TPD are summarized in Table 2 and Fig. 4. Table 2 shows the overall NH3-uptake, which represents the total amount of acidic sites and the NH3-uptake, that takes place from 150 to 500 °C and which reflects the amount of moderate acidic sites. Zeolite H-MFI 400, which was used as acidic component as well as support material, exhibited a total NH3-uptake of 0.48 mmol/gCat. With an uptake of 0.60 mmol/gCat, CZA-Z-CF shows the highest number of acidic sites. Since more than 50% of NH3-release takes place at temperatures above 500 °C, most of them can be considered as strong. Compared to the other catalysts, CZA-Z-CF shows the lowest percentage of NH3-release in the temperature range between 150 and 500 °C. The NH3-uptake of catalyst CZA-Z-CS is 0.52 mmol/gCat and NH3-release occurs, like in the case of catalyst CZA-Z-CF, predominantly at temperatures above 500 °C. Thus, its acid characteristics are similar to catalyst CZA-Z-CF. In contrast, catalyst CZA-Z-IP exhibits a comparatively low total NH3-uptake of 0.30 mmol/gCat and its amount of moderate acidic sites is also not very high. Catalyst CZA-Z-OX exhibits a total NH3-uptake of 0.40 mmol/gCat. However, the percentage of moderate acidic sites is the highest. The increase and decrease of zeolite acidity in bifunctional catalysts has been described by Flores et al. [40] and García-Trenco et al. [31]. According to Flores et al. CuO, ZnO and Al2O3 might migrate onto the zeolite leading to a blockage of acid sites. The increase can be explained by the formation of new Lewis-acid sites stemming from Al species of the CZA-component and this may be the case regarding CZA-Z-CF and CZA-Z-CS. García-Trenco used EPR-experiments to show that Cu2 + migrates to the zeolite and exchanges with zeolitic protons leading to a decrease in Brønsted-acidity.

Results of XRD measurements are displayed in Fig. 5, Fig. 6. Fig. 5 shows the diffraction patterns of the reference systems CZA (after calcination) and H-MFI 400. The diffraction patterns of the reduced, hence activated, bifunctional catalysts and CZA are summarized in Fig. 6. Some catalysts, like CZA-Z-IP, show narrow peaks and others, like CZA-Z-OX, show broader ones. The particle size of Cu was calculated by the Scherrer equation using the peak at 2θ ≈ 43° and the results are summarized in Table 3. The reference system and CZA-Z-OX both exhibit small Cu particles with diameters of 13.2 and 14.8 nm, respectively. The particle sizes of CZA-Z-CF and CZA-Z-CS are around 17.8 and 20.1 nm, respectively and thus slightly larger. CZA-Z-IP exhibits the largest Cu particle sizes around 39.9 nm.

The signal intensity for the zeolite reflections of CZA-Z-IP strongly differs from the other bifunctional catalysts. This might be due to the preparation method without any precipitating agent. Therefore, the pH could not be controlled and preparation occurred in an acidic reaction medium.

Table 4 summarizes the results of pulse chemisorption with N2O and values for metal dispersion, Cu surface area (SCu) and crystallite size are given for each catalyst system. The admixed catalyst CZA-Z exhibits a metal dispersion of 7% and a high Cu surface area of 10.46 m2/gSample. The corresponding SCu values for CZA-Z-CS and CZA-Z-OX are slightly higher. Compared to the other bifunctional catalysts, CZA-Z-OX shows the highest metal dispersion (8.76%), which is even higher than the metal dispersion of CZA-Z. The catalysts with the lowest metal dispersions and Cu surface areas are CZA-Z-CF and CZA-Z-IP. The former exhibits a metal dispersion of 4.56% and a Cu surface area of 6.58 m2/gSample. Regarding the latter, both values are further reduced and metal dispersion is below 1% while SCu is only 0.41 m2/gSample. A comparison between the Cu surface area estimated by N2O-pulse chemisorption with the specific surface area calculated by BET attests that catalysts with high surface areas do not necessarily display high metal dispersions. CZA-Z-CS for example exhibits a lower BET surface area (160 m2/g) than CZA-Z-CF (190 m2/g) but metal dispersion in the case of CZA-Z-CS (5.67%) is higher than in the case of CZA-Z-CF (4.56%).

The crystallite sizes were also calculated from the results of N2O-pulse chemisorption. As depicted in Table 4, the crystallite sizes of the catalysts increase in the following order: CZA-Z-OX < CZA-Z < CZA-Z-CS < CZA-Z-CF < CZA-Z-IP. The crystallite size of CZA-Z-IP was calculated to be larger than 300 nm. This can be explained by the very small Cu surface area, which leads to unreliable results. However, large particles of CZA-Z-IP can be assumed, which is also indicated by XRD. The crystallite sizes calculated by the Scherrer equation increase in the order CZA < CZA-Z-OX < CZA-Z-CF < CZA-Z-CS < CZA-Z-IP and thus differ slightly from the results of N2O-pulse chemisorption. However, the values obtained via the Scherrer equation should be considered as an estimation and together with the results from N2O-pulse chemisorption a general trend becomes visible.

TEM-images were recorded for the catalyst with the highest metal dispersion, CZA-Z-OX (Fig. 7). The sample is composed of a fine, nanoparticulate powder consisting of small agglomerated particles (mean particle size estimated from TEM images: < 10 nm; calculated mean: 7.2 ± 2.5 nm) and zeolite particles of larger size. Since the different ZnO, CuO and Al2O3 species cannot be clearly distinguished, an exact determination of the single particle sizes is not possible. From Fig. 7a it can be seen, that the CuO/ZnO/Al2O3 component and the zeolite are located closely to each other. However, there is only a minor occupation of CuO/ZnO/Al2O3 on the zeolite and both components appear rather independent from each other. High resolution TEM images (Fig. 7c and d) reveal the crystalline character of the CuO/ZnO/Al2O3 particles after calcination. The lattice spacings (indicated by arrows in Fig. 7d) are 0.275 nm, 0.277 nm and 0.232 nm identifying the (110) and the (111) planes of the CuO tenorite phase. The 0.281 nm, 0.262 nm and 0.245 spacings can be assigned to the (100), (002) and (101) planes of a hexagonal ZnO phase, respectively. STEM-HAADF images and EDX-analysis showed a homogeneous distribution of CuO, ZnO and Al2O3 within the hydrogenation catalyst.

Initially, a catalyst screening with respect to CO-conversion and selectivity was carried out (Fig. 8). Since the product distribution stayed constant with time on stream, the representative results shown in Fig. 8 refer to the values obtained at the end of the catalyst testing, i.e. after 14 h on stream. Under the applied reaction conditions and within the investigated time frame neither catalyst coking nor catalyst deactivation was observed.

Employing the admixed reference system CZA-Z, CO-conversion reached 48% and DME-selectivity was 69%. Hence, almost complete dehydration of methanol to DME took place. The study revealed that CZA-Z-OX is the only bifunctional catalyst that can compete with CZA-Z. CO-conversion was 45% and DME-selectivity reached 66%. Using CZA-Z-CS, moderate activity was observed. CO-conversion was 35% and since dehydration was almost complete, product selectivity was very good (66% DME-selectivity). In contrast, catalysts CZA-Z-CF and CZA-Z-IP showed low activity and CO-conversion was 17% and 10%, respectively. Regarding these two catalyst systems, a deviation in product selectivity was also observed. In the case of CZA-Z-IP, methanol dehydration was not complete and 9% of methanol was found in the product mixture. DME-selectivity was 61% and thus somewhat lower compared to the catalysts mentioned above. Employing CZA-Z-CF, DME-selectivity was only 38% and a considerable increase of CO2 − as well as hydrocarbons-formation was observed. Remarkable amounts of methanol were also observed in the product mixture.

To explain these phenomena it is necessary to correlate data from catalyst characterization with results from the catalyst screening. In this context, the influence of reduction temperature, surface area (BET), crystallite size and Cu surface area on CO-conversion was analyzed (Fig. 9). Regarding the influence of reduction temperature, i.e. reducibility of CuO, no significant influence on CO-conversion was observed. This is in accordance with the reduction curves shown in Fig. 3. The reduction curves prove that at 250 °C all CuO is reduced to Cu. Hence, under the reaction conditions described above, reduction is complete and reducibility of the catalysts does not influence catalytic activity. Considering the surface areas calculated by the BET method, a tendency to higher catalytic activity as a result of higher surface areas becomes visible. Regarding crystallite size and Cu surface area, there is a linear dependence of Cu surface area and an exponential dependence of crystallite size against CO-conversion. It should be noted that the crystallite size for CZA-Z-IP (Fig. 9, 10% CO-conversion) was taken from the Scherrer equation. Otherwise, crystallite sizes from N2O pulse chemisorption were used. Catalysts with high Cu surface areas and small crystallite sizes of Cu species are highly active and show highest CO-conversions. This is in accordance with several sophisticated studies on catalysts for methanol production [41], [42]. Jung et al. also described a strong influence of Cu surface area on catalytic activity for the single step synthesis of DME from synthesis gas [43].

The low activity of CZA-Z-CF and CZA-Z-IP can be explained by small Cu surface areas and comparatively large Cu crystallites. CZA-Z-IP exhibits the lowest Cu surface area, the largest Cu crystallites and the lowest BET surface area of all investigated catalysts. Accordingly, CO-conversion is only 10% and thus the lowest. Catalyst CZA-Z-CF exhibits a slightly higher activity and the results from catalyst testing can also be explained by its small Cu surface area and comparatively large Cu crystallites. The moderate activity of CZA-Z-CS does also correlate with these catalyst features. Regarding the admixed system CZA-Z and the bifunctional catalyst CZA-Z-OX, highest CO-conversions are observed as consequence of highest Cu surface areas and smallest crystallites. Furthermore, BET surface areas of these two catalyst systems are the highest.

All catalysts with good activity, i.e. CZA-Z, CZA-Z-CS and CZA-Z-OX, exhibited high DME-selectivity. Hence, high CO-conversion correlates with high DME-selectivity. In the case of CZA-Z-IP, that showed lowest CO-conversion, DME-selectivity is decreased to 61% and this can be ascribed to the low number of acidic sites (Table 2) leading to incomplete dehydration of methanol to DME. Concerning CZA-Z-CF, which gives a DME-selectivity of only 38%, the low percentage of moderate acidic sites (Table 2) might explain the comparatively high methanol content in the product mixture. Otherwise, this catalyst exhibits the highest percentage of strong acidic sites. This fact combined with the low catalytic activity of CZA-Z-CF enables side-reactions. Most probably, such strong acidic sites promote dehydration of DME to hydrocarbons, following mechanisms of the methanol-to-gasoline process [44]. Accordingly, a comparatively high hydrocarbon selectivity of 7% was observed. The increased amount of water can lead to higher WGS activity and this could explain the increased CO2-selectivity.

The results obtained with CZA-Z-IP indicate that the impregnation technique is not applicable for the preparation of bifunctional DME catalysts. Possibly, the absence of a precipitating agent leads to an acidic reaction medium, which affected the structure of the zeolite and its acidity. This is supported by the XRD reflections (Fig. 6) and by the results of NH3-TPD (Table 2). Furthermore, during the impregnation procedure the solvent evaporates, which can lead to the agglomeration of Cu species. This could explain the formation of comparatively large Cu crystallites as determined by N2O-pulse chemisorption. The drop in the surface area of CZA-Z-IP can be due to pore blockage during synthesis.

All other preparation methods included the use of a precipitating agent, which potentially prevented a change in the zeolite structure. For catalyst CZA-Z-CS, the formation of the copper- and zinc-hydroxycarbonates, which are formed during precipitation with Na2CO3, takes place in the absence of the zeolite. Hence, the co-precipitation sedimentation method is in its beginning identical to the common preparation of methanol catalysts. However, catalyst CZA-Z-CS, showed only moderate activity compared to the reference catalyst CZA-Z. Thus, it can be concluded that the second part of the preparation procedure, the sedimentation process, causes the loss in activity.

Regarding CZA-Z-CF and CZA-Z-OX, both catalysts have been prepared by co-precipitating the metal nitrates into a suspension of the zeolite. Different precipitating agents have been used and the observed differences in catalytic activity reveal a strong influence of the precipitating agents on the resulting catalytic performance. The influence of precipitating agent has also been investigated by Bae et al. [45]. The usage of oxalic acid instead of sodium carbonate is by far more favorable and the resulting catalyst CZA-Z-OX showed, according to N2O-pulse chemisorption and TEM analysis, a homogeneous distribution and a high dispersion of Cu species. Moreover, retention of the zeolite structure was confirmed by XRD and TEM. The TEM-images of CZA-Z-OX also showed that both catalytic components are located closely to each other and there is no evidence for blocking of catalytically active sites of the zeolite. Hence, acidity is not strongly affected as can be seen from the NH3-TPD results. It is known that the dehydration catalyst does not only influence product selectivity but also CO-conversion [32], [46]. Thus, retention of the zeolite structure in CZA-Z-OX together with its high Cu surface area and small Cu particle sizes leads to good catalytic activity.

Results obtained within this work indicate that catalyst features and activity strongly depend on the preparation method. Catalysts CZA-Z-CF and CZA-Z-IP, which were obtained via co-precipitation–impregnation and impregnation, respectively, exhibited low activity. Their small Cu surface areas, low metal dispersion and large crystallite sizes are certainly the main reasons for low CO-conversion. The combination of low activity and the presence of strong acidic sites in the case of CZA-Z-CF, resulted in an increased amount of side products, especially CO2, methanol and hydrocarbons. The use of catalyst CZA-Z-IP, which exhibited the lowest amount of acidic sites and the lowest catalytic activity, leads to incomplete dehydration of methanol to DME. However, promising results were obtained employing the bifunctional catalysts CZA-Z-CS and CZA-Z-OX, which were synthesized by co-precipitation-sedimentation and oxalate co-precipitation, respectively. Especially the latter method can be considered as an efficient synthesis strategy for zeolite-based bifunctional catalysts and the corresponding catalyst CZA-Z-OX enabled high CO-conversion, complete methanol dehydration and high DME-selectivity. Its performance is in agreement with various crucial characteristics like a high Cu surface area, small Cu particle sizes as well as a high number of moderate acidic sites. Thus, catalyst CZA-Z-OX can compete with conventional admixed catalyst systems. Future studies will imply further preparation methods and a deeper understanding of their influence on catalyst activity.
